name: Acro dance

narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

instructor.persona: A professional dancer with a background in both contemporary dance and circus arts.

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Acro dance emerged in the United States and Canada in the early 1900s within the vaudeville circuit.
It evolved from separate dance and acrobatic acts into a combined performance style.
Key figures include Sherman Coates, Tommy Woods, and Lulu Coates.
on_screen: Map: United States and Canada · Global

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Dancers perform in competitive dance, professional theater, and contemporary circus productions like Cirque du Soleil.
Today it remains a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Acro dance requires fluid transitions between dance steps and acrobatic tricks.
It relies on a foundation of ballet, jazz, or contemporary dance.
Tricks are categorized as solo, partner, known as adagio, or group, known as pyramids.
Watch for the Pitch tuck, Bridge pyramid, and Triple cartwheel.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (KeqgvrUKRkQ)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Solo, pair, or group formations; requires fluid transitions across the performance space.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers wear form-fitting clothing to ensure safety and showcase body lines.
Footwear includes jazz shoes or foot thongs to provide traction and cushioning on hard stages, unlike the foam-cushioned floors used in gymnastics.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Sherman Coates, Tommy Woods, Lulu Coates, and Miriam, the acrobatic tapper, shape this art.
It has origins in North America across the US and Canada, and is now practiced globally.
The style evolved from vaudeville variety acts into a modern discipline integrated with ballet and contemporary dance technique.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Acro dance is influenced by ballet, which provides the foundational technique for modern acro dance.
Acro dance is also influenced by jazz dance, serving as a primary foundation for acro dance movements.

music_brief.purpose: original soundtrack faithful to the tradition, with documented commercial reuse rights and no recurring royalties
music_brief.rights_rule: A composition brief does not clear an output. Record the provider/model/version, terms and date, input rights, output licence, restrictions and review before release.
music_brief.prompt: Original instrumental composition in the musical world of Acro dance (United States and Canada). New melody, new arrangement: do not quote or imitate any specific recorded song; keep the idiom, the instruments, the pulse and the proportions.

tracks.use: chapters: dance it to the music

rules: Original composition only — no sampling, no melody of any existing recording, no lyrics from any song.
Traditional public-domain tunes may be used only when the profile names them and a public-domain source is on file; otherwise compose new material in the idiom.
Keep the proportions true: the meter, the tempo range and the instrument roles the sources describe.
Label every generated track with the tool, the date and this brief, so provenance is always clear.

no caricature, no exaggeration, no mixing of regions or eras

The underside of a dancer's foot thong, showing the leather pads that cover the ball of the foot. The pads provide limited traction, yet have enough "slip" to allow turning (while protecting against skin abrasion). They also provide limited cushioning from hard impacts that can occur during leaps and acro dance tricks.
